newsitem.title: FRANCE: France disappointed by "spineless" Zaire reaction.
newsitem.headline: France disappointed by "spineless" Zaire reaction.

text.p: France accused the international community of being spineless on Wednesday as it vented frustration at the poor response to a proposed multinational force to help avert a refugee disaster in Zaire.

"I'm knocking on doors, asking if anyone is prepared to assume his responsibilities. The answer is 'Could you come back tomorrow', or 'We might lend an aircraft'," Foreign Minister Herve de Charette told LCI television.
"The main obstacle is the international community's spinelessness," he said.
President Jacques Chirac held a meeting with senior cabinet ministers on the Zaire crisis but presidential aides would not say what took place at the closed-door session.

France insists all major nations must participate in the force, which would help to get relief to more than one million refugees in eastern Zaire left without food by the fighting between Zairean troops and Rwanda-backed Tutsi rebels.

So far only Spain has responded, saying it would send fewer than 1,000 troops while Paris would despatch 1,000 to a force which needed to be at least 5,000 strong. Ethiopia said it was prepared to contribute troops to a neutral force proposed at an African summit on Tuesday.
De Charette said he still hoped the force could be put together. "It should already have been done," he added.
Defence Ministry sources said the military was making contingency plans for a possible intervention but had not begun readying any men or equipment.
They would not confirm media reports which said the plan involved taking control of the airports in Goma and Bukavu, seized by Tutsi rebels, to allow relief workers to resume aid to refugee camps.
United Nations special envoy Raymond Chretien said after visiting Zairean President Mobutu Sese Seko at his French Riviera villa that Mobutu supported sending a multinational force to Zaire.
He quoted Mobutu as saying he would do his utmost so that a unilateral ceasefire declared by Tutsi rebels fighting Zairean forces could hold in order to let the multinational force work.
The rebels, who are holding a swathe of eastern Zaire, said they wanted an African force to protect the refugees and opposed any intervention by troops from outside the region, including from France.
France intervened in the area in 1994 to end ethnic massacres, drawing charges from its allies that it was seeking to further its interests and from Tutsi-ruled Rwanda that it was protecting Hutus.

Paris disclosed on Wednesday that President Jacques Chirac's chief aide Dominique de Villepin held secret talks with Mobutu in Switzerland last week, shortly before France made its proposal for a mutinational force.
Mobutu, who has been away from Zaire since August for cancer treatment, made a rare and brief appearance for reporters before meeting Chretien. The 66-year-old leader looked thin and tired.
Zaire's ambassador to France, Baya Ramazani, said Mobutu was getting better and closely following the situation back home.
"The president will go back home in the next few days. The situation demands it," said Ramazani, adding that all Zairean government actions were taken in agreement with the president.
Mobutu's spokesman in Kinshasa, Samba Kabuya Lumuna, said no one knew exactly when the president would return.
